props.title: Barbarian Queen II: The Empress Strikes Back

sections.content: The peculiar saga of low-budget sword-and-sorcery exploitation continues with Barbarian Queen II: The Empress Strikes Back, a loose sequel to Barbarian Queen (1985) that epitomizes Roger Corman's assembly-line approach to B-movie production in the late 1980s. Like its predecessor, it follows the proven formula established by Conan the Barbarian (1982), but with significantly less budget and more gratuitous elements. The film represents the tail end of the sword-and-sorcery boom that dominated low-budget filmmaking throughout the 1980s.

sections.content: Director Joe Finley, working under Corman's notorious cost-cutting demands, delivers exactly what the exploitation market expected - action, minimal costume design, and recycled sets from other Argentinian-shot productions. The film follows the template of earlier Corman sword-and-sorcery productions like Deathstalker II (1987) and Sorceress (1982), maintaining the producer's philosophy of maximizing production value through creative resource management and strategic "borrowing" from more expensive films.

While Lana Clarkson made the original Barbarian Queen (1985) memorable, her absence here highlights how these films often struggled to maintain continuity between installments. This was common in the direct-to-video boom of the late 1980s and early 1990s, as seen in countless sequels like Deathstalker III (1988) and Deathstalker IV (1991), where maintaining the original cast was less important than simply getting product to market. SUBHEAD: The End of an Era

Barbarian Queen II (1990) marks the sunset of the sword-and-sorcery exploitation boom that began with The Sword and the Sorcerer (1982). By 1990, these productions were becoming increasingly rare as direct-to-video horror and martial arts films began dominating the low-budget market. The film serves as an interesting timestamp of this transition, showing how the genre's tropes had become fully codified and commercialized by the end of its run.
